name: Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy
aliases: autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy

reference.source: American Academy of Sleep Medicine ICSD-3 / epilepsy literature
clinicalPearls: Stereotyped hyperkinetic or dystonic seizures arising predominantly from sleep, often in clusters through the night
Attacks are brief, sudden and highly stereotyped for a given patient, distinguishing them from parasomnias
Seizures frequently originate in the frontal lobe, though other cortical origins occur
An autosomal dominant form is linked to mutations in neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit genes and others
Events emerge mainly from non-REM sleep and the patient may be aware during or immediately after them
Video-EEG and video polysomnography help separate it from NREM parasomnias and REM sleep behaviour disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy is a focal epilepsy in which seizures are strongly modulated by sleep, arising most often from mesial or other frontal regions and producing dramatic hyperkinetic, dystonic or ambulatory motor behaviour. In the inherited form, mutations affecting neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and related genes alter cholinergic modulation of the sleep-wake and arousal networks, lowering the threshold for seizures during non-REM sleep. The stereotypy and brevity of events reflect their epileptic rather than parasomnic origin.
additionalDifferentials: NREM parasomnias (sleepwalking, sleep terrors, confusional arousals)
additionalInvestigations: Video-EEG and video polysomnography to capture and characterise events
MRI of the brain to seek a structural focus
Detailed semiological description and event stereotypy assessment
Genetic evaluation where an autosomal dominant pattern is present
redFlags: Frequent nocturnal clusters causing injury or major sleep disruption
Daytime seizures or new focal neurological signs
Diagnostic uncertainty between seizures and parasomnia
reference.prognosis: Seizures often respond to antiseizure medication, though a proportion are drug-resistant; the disorder is typically lifelong but many patients achieve good control.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing stereotyped nocturnal seizures as parasomnias or psychiatric events
Relying on routine daytime EEG, which is often normal
Overlooking a family history pointing to the inherited form
Failing to capture events with video for accurate classification
references: American Academy of Sleep Medicine ICSD-3
Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Control the nocturnal focal seizures with antiseizure medication, with carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine often effective, titrated against the clustering of events
Confirm the diagnosis with video-EEG and video polysomnography to distinguish it from parasomnias and guide treatment
Evaluate for a resectable structural focus and consider epilepsy surgery in drug-resistant cases
Optimise sleep and avoid seizure precipitants such as sleep deprivation
Offer genetic counselling where an autosomal dominant neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor form is identified
Provide multidisciplinary neurology and sleep medicine follow-up with counselling on driving and nocturnal safety
